title: Nehemiah 6:1–14
context: With the wall nearly complete, Nehemiah's enemies try to stop him by other means. Sanballat and Geshem repeatedly invite him to a meeting at Ono, intending to harm him, and he refuses each time. Sanballat then sends an open letter accusing him of plotting rebellion and appointing prophets to proclaim him king. Finally Shemaiah, hired by Tobiah and Sanballat, urges him to hide in the temple, but Nehemiah discerns the trap and refuses. He commits his enemies, including the prophetess Noadiah, to God.

verses.text: Now when it was reported to Sanballat, Tobiah, Geshem the Arabian, and to the rest of our enemies that I had built the wall, and that there was no breach left in it (though even to that time I had not set up the doors in the gates),
verses.arminianNotes: Sanballat, Tobiah, Geshem, and others hear that the wall is built with no breach left, though the doors are not yet set. Arminian readers note that progress provokes fresh opposition, a pattern faithful workers should expect.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that these same enemies appear in Nehemiah 2:19 and 4:7. Their persistence shows that opposition to God's work often intensifies as the work nears completion.

verses.text: Sanballat and Geshem sent to me, saying, “Come! Let’s meet together in the villages in the plain of Ono.” But they intended to harm me.
verses.arminianNotes: Sanballat and Geshem invite him to meet in the plain of Ono, “But they intended to harm me.” Arminian readers note Nehemiah's discernment, recognizing danger behind a friendly invitation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrator tells us their intent plainly. Nehemiah's wisdom guards both his life and the work entrusted to him.

verses.text: I sent messengers to them, saying, “I am doing a great work, so that I can’t come down. Why should the work cease while I leave it and come down to you?”
verses.arminianNotes: “I am doing a great work, so that I can’t come down.” Arminian readers see a leader who chooses to stay faithful to his calling rather than be drawn away by distraction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Nehemiah measures the invitation against the importance of the work God gave him. Some requests are best refused because they would halt what God has called us to do.

verses.text: They sent to me four times like this; and I answered them the same way.
verses.arminianNotes: They send four times, and he answers the same way. Arminian readers note the steady resolve of a man who does not wear down under repeated pressure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the persistence of the enemies and the consistency of Nehemiah's answer. Faithfulness often means giving the same answer again and again.

verses.text: Then Sanballat sent his servant to me the same way the fifth time with an open letter in his hand,
verses.arminianNotes: Sanballat sends a fifth time, now with “an open letter in his hand.” Arminian readers note that an open letter could be read by anyone, spreading the accusation it contained.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the change in method escalates the pressure. A public accusation aims to damage Nehemiah's reputation and stir fear among the people.

verses.text: in which was written, “It is reported among the nations, and Gashmu says it, that you and the Jews intend to rebel. Because of that, you are building the wall. You would be their king, according to these words.
verses.arminianNotes: The letter claims it is reported, "and Gashmu says it," that Nehemiah plans to rebel and be king. Arminian readers see slander used as a weapon, an attempt to frighten him into a meeting.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the same charge of rebellion was raised in Nehemiah 2:19. False accusation is a recurring tactic against God's servants.

verses.text: You have also appointed prophets to proclaim of you at Jerusalem, saying, ‘There is a king in Judah!’ Now it will be reported to the king according to these words. Come now therefore, and let’s take counsel together.”
verses.arminianNotes: The letter claims he has appointed prophets to proclaim, "There is a king in Judah!" Arminian readers note that the accusation threatens to bring the Persian king's anger on Nehemiah and the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the charge is crafted to seem dangerous to the empire. The invitation to "take counsel together" is the same trap in new clothing.

verses.text: Then I sent to him, saying, “There are no such things done as you say, but you imagine them out of your own heart.”
verses.arminianNotes: "There are no such things done as you say, but you imagine them out of your own heart." Arminian readers see a calm and direct denial, refusing to be drawn into defending himself further.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Nehemiah names the lie for what it is without being intimidated. A clear conscience allows a simple and firm reply.

verses.text: For they all would have made us afraid, saying, “Their hands will be weakened from the work, that it not be done.” But now, strengthen my hands.
verses.arminianNotes: They meant to make the people afraid so the work would stop. "But now, strengthen my hands." Arminian readers note that Nehemiah turns from the threat to prayer, asking God for strength to continue.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the brief prayer is typical of Nehemiah. Psalm 56:3 expresses the same response: "When I am afraid, I will put my trust in you."

verses.text: I went to the house of Shemaiah the son of Delaiah the son of Mehetabel, who was shut in at his home; and he said, “Let us meet together in God’s house, within the temple, and let’s shut the doors of the temple; for they will come to kill you. Yes, in the night they will come to kill you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Shemaiah, shut in at his home, urges him to hide in the temple and shut the doors, "for they will come to kill you." Arminian readers note how the danger now comes through a voice claiming to speak for God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the plot now uses religious language and the setting of God's house. Deception wrapped in spiritual authority is especially hard to resist.

verses.text: I said, “Should a man like me flee? Who is there that, being such as I, would go into the temple to save his life? I will not go in.”
verses.arminianNotes: "Should a man like me flee? Who is there that, being such as I, would go into the temple to save his life? I will not go in." Arminian readers see courage and integrity, refusing to act from fear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Nehemiah was not a priest, and the law guarded the sanctuary from those not appointed to it (Numbers 18:7). Entering would have been both cowardice and trespass.

verses.text: I discerned, and behold, God had not sent him, but he pronounced this prophecy against me. Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him.
verses.arminianNotes: Nehemiah discerned that "God had not sent him"; Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him. Arminian readers note that discernment is needed even with those who claim to speak for God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that a message contrary to God's word reveals its true source. John later urges believers to "test the spirits, whether they are of God" (1 John 4:1).

verses.text: He was hired so that I would be afraid, do so, and sin, and that they might have material for an evil report, that they might reproach me.
verses.arminianNotes: He was hired so Nehemiah would "be afraid, do so, and sin," giving material for an evil report. Arminian readers see that the goal was to draw Nehemiah into a sinful choice and discredit him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the plot aimed at Nehemiah's integrity as much as his life. Sin, not danger, was the real threat, and he recognized it.

verses.text: “Remember, my God, Tobiah and Sanballat according to these their works, and also the prophetess Noadiah and the rest of the prophets that would have put me in fear.”
verses.arminianNotes: Nehemiah prays, “Remember, my God, Tobiah and Sanballat according to these their works,” naming also “the prophetess Noadiah.” Arminian readers note that he leaves judgment to God rather than taking revenge himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the prayer resembles Nehemiah 4:4–5, where he asks God to deal with those who insulted the builders. He entrusts his enemies to God's justice.
